title: Nintendo Platforming Foundations
blurb: Nintendo's own console-defining run, joined by Rare's technically dazzling Donkey Kong Country trilogy.
games: The SNES pack-in that redefined the platformer with Yoshi, the world map, and secret exits — Europe waited about two years after Japan's 1990 launch title release.
A hand-drawn, crayon-and-watercolor art style wrapped around one of the most inventive platformers Nintendo ever built, released the same year worldwide.
16-bit remakes of all four NES Mario games in one cartridge, released simultaneously across Japan, North America, and Europe.
Pre-rendered CGI models pushed the SNES's graphics further than almost anything else on the system, reviving the Donkey Kong brand from scratch.
Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest
A darker pirate-themed sequel widely considered the series' peak, released the same year in all three regions.
Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!
The trilogy's closer, trading some of the pirate theming for a swampy, inventive final adventure.
Eight compact sub-games in one cartridge, including the two-player Helper system that let a friend control a captured enemy ability.
One of the SNES's final first-party releases, arriving so late in the console's life that a European release never materialized.
A golf-meets-pinball hybrid where Kirby himself is the ball, an unusually experimental format for the character.

title: Action-Adventure & Metroidvania
blurb: A Link to the Past and Super Metroid anchor a chapter full of Quintet's atmospheric action-RPGs, one of which never left Japan under its English name until a year after release.
games: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past
The template for nearly every top-down Zelda that followed, including the Dark World mechanic that doubled the game's map.
Widely considered the high point of 2D Metroid, released the same year worldwide and still cited as a genre-defining Metroidvania.
An atmospheric action-RPG following a boy's journey around a fictionalized real-world map, released in Japan as Gaia Gensouki the year before.
Released in Japan as Tenchi Sōzō the year before — this one never received a North American release at all, one of the most requested unlocalized SNES RPGs ever.
An unusual reversal: this action-RPG was developed entirely by Square's North American studio and never released in Japan at all.
A genre hybrid alternating side-scrolling action with light city-building sim sections, released in Europe the same year as North America.
Quintet's earlier action-RPG about resurrecting a ruined world town by town, with Europe's release following about a year later.
A moody, atmospheric spin-off starring Ghosts 'n Goblins' gargoyle antihero Firebrand, released in Europe the year after North America.
The Legend of the Mystical Ninja
A Ganbare Goemon spin-off with Goemon and Ebisumaru renamed Kid Ying and Dr. Yang outside Japan, released the same year in all three regions.

title: Role-Playing Adventures
blurb: Square and Enix's golden age, and the platform where the console RPG genre truly matured — several of these never received any European release at all.
games: Widely regarded as one of the best RPGs ever made, pairing time travel with a New Game+ structure years ahead of its time — never released in Europe on SNES.
Released in North America as Final Fantasy III, since only two earlier entries had reached the West at the time — no European SNES release ever happened.
Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars
Square and Nintendo's first collaboration, blending Mario's world with turn-based, timed-hit combat — never released in Europe.
Released in Japan as Mother 2 a year earlier, with a deliberately mundane, present-day setting that stood out against typical fantasy RPGs — never released in Europe.
A real-time action-RPG built around a cooperative three-player mode, released in Europe the year after North America.
Capcom's own entry into the console RPG genre, released in Europe about a year after its North American debut.
A direct sequel deepening the original's dragon-transformation mechanics — never released in Europe.
The first entry in the long-running Tales series — a Japan-only SNES release that never reached the West on this platform at all.
An anthology RPG spanning wildly different historical eras and playable characters — Japan-only until an official Western localization finally arrived in 2022, 28 years later.

title: Run-and-Gun & Shooters
blurb: Konami's Contra and Gradius sequels anchor a chapter full of genuinely difficult SNES shoot-em-ups, several carrying real regional title changes.
games: Renamed Super Probotector: Alien Rebels in Europe, continuing the same robot-reskin censorship pattern the series carried on NES.
A launch-window SNES port of the brutally difficult arcade shoot-em-up, released the same year across all three regions.
A vertical shooter alternating between two visual styles stage to stage, showing off the SNES's Mode 7 scaling technique.
A home port of the arcade sequel, arriving in the West about two years after its original Japanese release.
Renamed Space Megaforce for its North American release, while Europe kept the original Japanese title, Super Aleste — a rare case of only one Western region getting a new name.
Released in Japan the year before as Assault Suits Valken, with some story content trimmed for the Western Cybernator release.
An obscure but well-regarded ninja run-and-gun-platformer hybrid, reaching the West about a year after its Japanese release.
A home conversion of Konami's cowboy-themed arcade run-and-gun, released the same year across regions.

title: Beat-em-ups, Wrestling & Fighting
blurb: Capcom's Final Fight trilogy and Street Fighter II's SNES ports anchor a chapter that also includes one game with three genuinely different regional titles.
games: An enhanced SNES-exclusive revision adding faster gameplay and the four boss characters as playable fighters.
Adds four new challengers to the roster, released the same year across all three regions.
A home port of the arcade sequel, restoring blood via a code — unlike the heavily censored first game's SNES port.
A home conversion of Capcom's arcade beat-em-up landmark, released in Europe the year after Japan.
A SNES-original sequel skipping arcades entirely, released the same year across regions.
The trilogy's closer, adding selectable special moves and a genuinely large character roster for the genre.
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles IV: Turtles in Time
Released in Europe as Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles IV, continuing the same UK broadcast-driven rename the franchise carried on other platforms.
Released in Japan as Rushing Beat Ran and in Europe as Rival Turf! 2, tying it to an earlier Jaleco beat-em-up despite no such numbering in Japan or North America.
An unusually scattered regional rollout: Japan's The Ninja Warriors Again, North America's plain The Ninja Warriors, and Europe's Ninja Warriors: The New Generation are all the same game.

title: Puzzle & Party
blurb: A Japan-only Panel de Pon became Tetris Attack for a Western audience that had no idea it wasn't really a Tetris game at all.
games: Originally Japan's character-driven puzzler Panel de Pon a year earlier — the Western version swapped in Yoshi's Island characters and was branded around Tetris despite having no real connection to it.
A Western-exclusive reskin of Super Puyo Puyo with Kirby's cast replacing the original characters — the only Kirby game never released in Japan.
An unusual case where the North American release actually preceded the Japanese one by about a month.
A four-player-capable entry that helped define the series' multiplayer battle format for the 16-bit era.
Adds new power-ups and battle stages, released in the West about a year after Japan.
A British-developed platformer-puzzler hybrid about a detachable-limbed hero, released the same year in all three regions.
A unicycle racer built entirely around chained stunt tricks, released in Europe the following year as Unirally — never released in Japan.
This SNES version is distinct from the earlier NES release — Japan only ever got it via the Satellaview satellite service, never a retail cartridge.

title: Sports & Racing
blurb: F-Zero and Super Mario Kart's Mode 7 tracks anchor a chapter that also holds a surprising number of American-sports titles that made it to Europe anyway.
games: A launch-window showcase for the SNES's Mode 7 pseudo-3D scaling, and one of the earliest anti-gravity racers.
The kart-racing genre's true origin point, released the same year across all three regions.
A flight-sim-adjacent launch title built to show off Mode 7's scaling and rotation effects, Europe following about a year after Japan.
Released in Japan as Top Racer, a Mode 7 racer built by a British studio, published the same year across regions.
An overhead combat racer from the studio that would later become Blizzard Entertainment, released only in the West.
A home conversion of the arcade basketball hit, released across Japan, North America, and Europe the same year — despite being an American sport.
Ken Griffey Jr. Presents Major League Baseball
A North America-exclusive baseball title, never released in Japan or Europe.
Released in Japan under different NFL-free branding, this American-football sim still found its way to a genuine European PAL release.
A soccer sim released in the West about a year after its Japanese debut, notably getting a real North American release despite the sport's smaller US audience.

title: Simulation & Strategy
blurb: SimCity's SNES port anchors a small chapter that includes three tactical RPGs that stayed in Japan for years, or forever.
games: A console-exclusive redesign of the PC city-builder with a Mario-themed bonus mode, released the same year across all three regions.
One of the SNES's last major releases anywhere, launching the farming-sim genre with a full day-and-season cycle.
Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen
A tactics-RPG hybrid built around real-time troop movement across a war map, reaching North America two years after Japan — never released in Europe.
A mecha tactical RPG that launched a long-running series — Japan-only on SNES; the West wouldn't see the franchise until later entries on other platforms.
Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together
A landmark tactical RPG, Japan-only on SNES — its first Western release came three years later on PlayStation, deliberately timed to avoid clashing with Final Fantasy Tactics.
An Age-of-Exploration trading and naval-combat sim, released in North America the same year as Japan — never released in Europe.
A British-developed god-game classic, ported to SNES the same year across all three regions.

title: Licensed, Movie & TV Tie-ins
blurb: Capcom and Konami's Disney and superhero tie-ins remain some of the best-regarded licensed games of the 16-bit era.
games: Widely considered one of the best licensed platformers ever made, released in North America the year before its European and Japanese debuts.
A famously difficult platformer built around the film's key scenes, released across Europe and North America the same year.
A beat-em-up/platformer hybrid tied to the Tim Burton sequel, released the same year across all three regions.
A cooperative puzzle-adventure directed by a young Shinji Mikami, years before he created Resident Evil.
A British-developed platformer that reached North America about eight months before its own European release.
Tiny Toon Adventures: Buster Busts Loose!
A well-regarded platformer starring the Tiny Toons cast, released in Europe about six months after Japan.
A licensed beat-em-up/platformer letting players swap between five X-Men, released in Europe the year after North America.
A licensed tie-in blending on-foot action with first-person raptor-hunting sections, released the same year worldwide.
The Great Circus Mystery Starring Mickey & Minnie
Released in Japan as Magical Adventure 2 — unusually, Europe's release actually preceded North America's by a few months.

title: Cult Classics & Deep Cuts
blurb: Earthworm Jim's absurdist run-and-gun sits alongside a run of Japan-only Square and Human Entertainment titles that stayed unlocalized for decades.
games: A surreal run-and-gun starring a sentient earthworm in a robotic supersuit, released the same year across Europe and North America.
A stranger, more level-design-experimental sequel, released in Europe the year after North America.
A cooperative horror-comedy shooter parodying B-movie monster tropes, released the same year across Europe and North America.
Drops the original's city-building sections entirely in favor of pure action, released in Europe the year after North America.
A pioneering point-and-click survival horror game, Japan-only on SNES — its own sequel wouldn't reach the West until PlayStation, years later.
A tactical RPG with dragon-riding mechanics, never officially localized anywhere — only reachable through a long-standing fan translation.
The series' Japan-only SNES debut — the West's first taste of it came 12 years later via a PSP remake.
A cult physics-platformer built entirely around a stretchy fishing line, Japan-only on SNES and largely unknown in the West for decades.
Released in Japan as Slapstick, this robot-building RPG reached North America the same year — but never Europe.

title: More RPGs & Genre Hybrids
blurb: A second helping of console RPGs and genre-blending curios, several of which stopped at North America and never crossed to Europe.
games: Released in Japan as Elnard, this six-hero RPG reached North America the same year — but never Europe.
Released in Japan as Estpolis Denki, launching a series that would return with a well-regarded prequel two years later — never released in Europe.
Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals
A prequel widely considered a major leap over the original, reaching North America the year after its Japanese release.
An evolution-themed action-RPG letting players guide a creature from fish to dinosaur to mammal — never released in Europe.
A home port of the rotoscoped PC platformer classic, released the same year across all three regions.
A cyberpunk-fantasy RPG based on the tabletop game — a completely separate, unrelated adaptation from the same-year Sega Genesis game sharing its name and license.

title: Multiplayer, Novelty & Peripheral Games
blurb: Argonaut's Super FX chip games anchor a chapter closing on Star Fox 2, a finished game that didn't officially ship until 2017.
games: A mouse-and-pad peripheral bundle turning the SNES into a drawing and music-composition tool, released the same year worldwide.
A light-gun peripheral bundle of six mini-games, with North America getting the Super Scope itself before Japan or Europe.
Released in Japan as Wild Trax, this Super FX chip-powered racer used chunky 3D polygon models years before it was common on consoles.
The Super FX chip's flagship showcase, turning the SNES into a passable 3D rail-shooter machine, released the same year worldwide.

Completed and ready to ship in 1995, then shelved when Nintendo judged its visuals would look dated next to the incoming PlayStation and Saturn — it finally released 22 years later, bundled with the SNES Classic Edition.

A heavily censored SNES port removing Nazi imagery and blood entirely to meet Nintendo's content policy — a striking contrast to the uncensored PC original, which was itself restricted in Germany for decades.
A technically ambitious port of id Software's FPS landmark, built to run on hardware never designed for it — a genuine engineering feat even with the compromises required.
The infamous SNES port that removed blood entirely under Nintendo's content policy — the Sega Genesis version's now-legendary blood code had no SNES equivalent.
